claim: Cerebellar Purkinje cells control eye movements with a rapid rate code.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje cells control eye movements with a rapid rate code that is invariant to spike irregularity
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported throughout the manuscript by recording, stimulation, and modeling data.

claim: The rate code used by cerebellar Purkinje cells to control eye movements is invariant to spike irregularity.
source: Cerebellar Purkinje cells control eye movements with a rapid rate code that is invariant to spike irregularity
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported by experimental data showing no additional contribution of spike irregularity beyond spike rate.

claim: During oculomotor behavior in mice and rhesus monkeys, mean irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking varied with mean eye velocity.
source: Accordingly, during oculomotor behavior in mice and rhesus monkeys, mean irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking varied with mean eye velocity.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Moment-to-moment variations revealed a tight correlation between eye velocity and spike rate, with no additional information conveyed by spike irregularity.
source: However, moment-to-moment variations revealed a tight correlation between eye velocity and spike rate, with no additional information conveyed by spike irregularity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by residual analysis in Figure 2 and linear mixed effects modeling.

claim: When spike rate and irregularity were independently controlled using optogenetic stimulation, the eye movements elicited were well-described by a linear population rate code with 3–5 ms temporal precision.
source: Moreover, when spike rate and irregularity were independently controlled using optogenetic stimulation, the eye movements elicited were well-described by a linear population rate code with 3–5 ms temporal precision.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments in Figures 3-5.

claim: Biophysical and random-walk models identified biologically realistic parameter ranges that determine whether spike irregularity influences responses downstream.
source: Biophysical and random-walk models identified biologically realistic parameter ranges that determine whether spike irregularity influences responses downstream.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling in Figures 7-9.

claim: The results demonstrate cerebellar control of movements through a remarkably rapid rate code, with no evidence for an additional contribution of spike irregularity.
source: The results demonstrate cerebellar control of movements through a remarkably rapid rate code, with no evidence for an additional contribution of spike irregularity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by all experimental and modeling results.

claim: Action potentials, or spikes, are the primary language used by the nervous system.
source: Action potentials, or spikes, are the primary language used by the nervous system.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Throughout the brain, the rate at which neurons fire spikes encodes information.
source: Throughout the brain, the rate at which neurons fire spikes encodes information (Adrian, 1928; Kuffler, 1951; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Wright et al., 1967; reviewed in Borst and Theunissen, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The rate at which neurons fire spikes affects the activity of downstream neurons.
source: Throughout the brain, the rate at which neurons fire spikes encodes information (Adrian, 1928; Kuffler, 1951; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Wright et al., 1967; reviewed in Borst and Theunissen, 1999), affects the activity of downstream neurons (Tsodyks and Markram, 1997; Bagnall et al., 2008; Turecek et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rate at which neurons fire spikes drives motor output.
source: Throughout the brain, the rate at which neurons fire spikes encodes information (Adrian, 1928; Kuffler, 1951; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Wright et al., 1967; reviewed in Borst and Theunissen, 1999), affects the activity of downstream neurons (Tsodyks and Markram, 1997; Bagnall et al., 2008; Turecek et al., 2016), and drives motor output (Crowell et al., 1968; Evarts, 1968; Evarts, 1969; Henn and Cohen, 1976; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Hanes and Schall, 1996; reviewed in Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A rate code is widely used for neural computation.
source: Throughout the brain, the rate at which neurons fire spikes encodes information (Adrian, 1928; Kuffler, 1951; Hubel and Wiesel, 1959; Wright et al., 1967; reviewed in Borst and Theunissen, 1999), affects the activity of downstream neurons (Tsodyks and Markram, 1997; Bagnall et al., 2008; Turecek et al., 2016), and drives motor output (Crowell et al., 1968; Evarts, 1968; Evarts, 1969; Henn and Cohen, 1976; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Hanes and Schall, 1996; reviewed in Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017), indicating that a rate code is widely used for neural computation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about rate coding throughout the brain.

claim: The precise temporal pattern of spikes can encode information beyond that carried by spike rate.
source: In addition, the precise temporal pattern of spikes can encode information beyond that carried by spike rate, suggesting that a temporal code may also contribute to information processing (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Theunissen and Miller, 1995; Gawne et al., 1996; de Ruyter van Steveninck et al., 1997; Stopfer et al., 1997; Victor, 1999; Stopfer and Laurent, 1999; Reich et al., 2000; Panzeri et al., 2001; Huxter et al., 2003; Butts et al., 2007; Engineer et al., 2008; Gollisch and Meister, 2008; Huxter et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: It is not clear whether and how information encoded in the temporal pattern of spikes is transmitted to downstream circuits to influence behavior.
source: However, it is not clear whether and how information encoded in the temporal pattern of spikes is transmitted to downstream circuits to influence behavior.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Previous work has analyzed both types of spike timing (precise timing within individual neurons and relative timing across neurons) in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: In the cerebellum, previous work has analyzed both types of spike timing in Purkinje cells, which are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Person and Raman, 2012a; Steuber and Jaeger, 2013; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; reviewed in De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Person and Raman, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex.
source: In the cerebellum, previous work has analyzed both types of spike timing in Purkinje cells, which are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex (Person and Raman, 2012a; Steuber and Jaeger, 2013; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; reviewed in De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Person and Raman, 2012b).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: It has been hypothesized that the irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking affects the cerebellar control of movements.
source: It has been hypothesized that the irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking affects the cerebellar control of movements (reviewed in De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The irregularity of the interspike intervals (ISIs) is a temporal feature of spike trains that varies along a continuum across brain regions and across individual neurons.
source: The irregularity of the interspike intervals (ISIs) is a temporal feature of spike trains that varies along a continuum across brain regions and across individual neurons (Maimon and Assad, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In a given neuron, the level of spike irregularity can vary as the neuron processes information.
source: Further, in a given neuron, the level of spike irregularity can vary as the neuron processes information (Barlow and Levick, 1969; Young et al., 1988; de Ruyter van Steveninck et al., 1997; Fairhall et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In Purkinje cells, spontaneous spiking is more regular than a Poisson process.
source: In Purkinje cells, spontaneous spiking is more regular than a Poisson process (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Shin et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spike irregularity in Purkinje cells can vary during the processing of sensory signals.
source: In Purkinje cells, spontaneous spiking is more regular than a Poisson process (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Shin et al., 2007), and spike irregularity can vary during the processing of sensory signals (Shin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pathological alteration of the spike irregularity of Purkinje cells has been proposed as a potential cause of ataxia and other cerebellum-related disorders such as autism.
source: Moreover, pathological alteration of the spike irregularity of Purkinje cells has been proposed as a potential cause of ataxia and other cerebellum-related disorders such as autism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work that the current study tests.

claim: In several different mouse models of ataxia, Purkinje cell spiking is more irregular than in normal Purkinje cells.
source: In several different mouse models of ataxia (Hoebeek et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2006; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Stahl and Thumser, 2014; Mark et al., 2015; Jayabal et al., 2016) and autism (Peter et al., 2016), Purkinje cell spiking is more irregular than in normal Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: In mouse models of autism, Purkinje cell spiking is more irregular than in normal Purkinje cells.
source: In several different mouse models of ataxia (Hoebeek et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2006; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Stahl and Thumser, 2014; Mark et al., 2015; Jayabal et al., 2016) and autism (Peter et al., 2016), Purkinje cell spiking is more irregular than in normal Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increases in the regularity of Purkinje cell spiking, caused by reductions in inhibitory synaptic input, have been associated with motor deficits.
source: Moreover, increases in the regularity of Purkinje cell spiking, caused by reductions in inhibitory synaptic input (Wulff et al., 2009) or maternal exposure to cannabinoids (Shabani et al., 2011), have also been associated with motor deficits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increases in the regularity of Purkinje cell spiking, caused by maternal exposure to cannabinoids, have been associated with motor deficits.
source: Moreover, increases in the regularity of Purkinje cell spiking, caused by reductions in inhibitory synaptic input (Wulff et al., 2009) or maternal exposure to cannabinoids (Shabani et al., 2011), have also been associated with motor deficits.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Observations of increased or decreased spike irregularity in Purkinje cells in mouse models of ataxia have inspired the hypothesis that any perturbation of normal spike irregularity may impair the ability of Purkinje cells to reliably transmit information for the control of movement.
source: Such observations of increased or decreased spike irregularity in Purkinje cells in mouse models of ataxia have inspired the hypothesis that any perturbation of normal spike irregularity may impair the ability of Purkinje cells to reliably transmit information for the control of movement (Hoebeek et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2006; Wulff et al., 2009; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Luthman et al., 2011; De Zeeuw et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work supported by multiple citations.

claim: Computer modeling has identified short-term synaptic depression as one potential mechanism that would allow spike irregularity in Purkinje cells to influence their control of postsynaptic targets.
source: Computer modeling has identified short-term synaptic depression as one potential mechanism that would allow spike irregularity in Purkinje cells to influence their control of postsynaptic targets.
evidence: This is a finding from prior computational modeling work.

claim: Irregular presynaptic spike trains contain short ISIs that recruit more short-term depression.
source: Because irregular presynaptic spike trains contain short ISIs that recruit more short-term depression, short-term depression has the potential to reduce the mean synaptic conductance in the postsynaptic target during more irregular spike trains (Luthman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Short-term depression has the potential to reduce the mean synaptic conductance in the postsynaptic target during more irregular spike trains.
source: Because irregular presynaptic spike trains contain short ISIs that recruit more short-term depression, short-term depression has the potential to reduce the mean synaptic conductance in the postsynaptic target during more irregular spike trains (Luthman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a prediction from prior modeling work supported by a citation.

claim: Causal evidence for a direct contribution of irregularity to impaired motor control is mixed.
source: However, causal evidence for a direct contribution of irregularity to impaired motor control is mixed.
evidence: This summarizes the state of evidence from prior work.

claim: In mouse models of ataxia, treatments that reverse the abnormally high irregularity have reversed motor deficits in some cases.
source: In mouse models of ataxia, treatments that reverse the abnormally high irregularity have reversed motor deficits in some cases (Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Walter et al., 2006; Jayabal et al., 2016), but not others (Stahl and Thumser, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mouse models of ataxia, treatments that reverse the abnormally high irregularity have not reversed motor deficits in some cases.
source: In mouse models of ataxia, treatments that reverse the abnormally high irregularity have reversed motor deficits in some cases (Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Walter et al., 2006; Jayabal et al., 2016), but not others (Stahl and Thumser, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The severity of motor deficits in different mouse lines does not always correspond to the severity of the perturbation of Purkinje cell spike irregularity in the relevant region of the cerebellum.
source: Moreover, the severity of motor deficits in different mouse lines does not always correspond to the severity of the perturbation of Purkinje cell spike irregularity in the relevant region of the cerebellum (Stahl and Thumser, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Floccular Purkinje cells are located just two synapses from the motor neurons that innervate the eye muscles.
source: Located just two synapses from the motor neurons that innervate the eye muscles, floccular Purkinje cells are a key node in the sensorimotor transformation of visual and vestibular signals into oculomotor commands.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the oculomotor circuit.

claim: Floccular Purkinje cells are a key node in the sensorimotor transformation of visual and vestibular signals into oculomotor commands.
source: Located just two synapses from the motor neurons that innervate the eye muscles, floccular Purkinje cells are a key node in the sensorimotor transformation of visual and vestibular signals into oculomotor commands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the functional role of floccular Purkinje cells.

claim: Recording and stimulation studies in a range of species have established an influence of Purkinje cell spike rate on eye movement behavior.
source: Recording and stimulation studies in a range of species have established an influence of Purkinje cell spike rate on eye movement behavior (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Noda and Suzuki, 1979; Stone and Lisberger, 1990; Lisberger et al., 1994; Lisberger, 1994; Kahlon and Lisberger, 1999; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013; Katoh et al., 2015; Kodama and du Lac, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The possibility that the spike irregularity of floccular Purkinje cells might influence eye movements has been suggested by the observation of abnormal oculomotor behavior or oculomotor learning in mouse models of ataxia with abnormal Purkinje cell spike irregularity.
source: The possibility that the spike irregularity of floccular Purkinje cells might also influence eye movements has been suggested by the observation of abnormal oculomotor behavior or oculomotor learning in mouse models of ataxia with abnormal Purkinje cell spike irregularity (Hoebeek et al., 2005; Katoh et al., 2007; Katoh et al., 2008; Wulff et al., 2009; Stahl and Thumser, 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis suggested by prior observations, supported by citations.

claim: The spike rate of a majority of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar flocculus and ventral paraflocculus encode gaze velocity.
source: It is well established that the spike rate of a majority of Purkinje cells in this region of the cerebellum encode gaze velocity (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1974; Lisberger et al., 1994; Pastor et al., 1997; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Hirata and Highstein, 2000; Katoh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The spike rate of Purkinje cells in the sample was highly correlated with gaze velocity during visual tracking with the head stationary.
source: Consistent with previous work (Lisberger and Fuchs, 1978; Lisberger et al., 1994; Pastor et al., 1997; Raymond and Lisberger, 1998; Hirata and Highstein, 2001; Katoh et al., 2015), the spike rate of Purkinje cells in our samples was highly correlated with gaze velocity. Gaze velocity is defined as the angular velocity of the eye in world coordinates, which is equal to the sum of eye velocity in the head, plus head velocity in the world. When animals tracked a moving visual stimulus with the head stationary, gaze velocity was equal to eye velocity, and there was a clear correlation between Purkinje cell spike rate and gaze velocity, in both the population mean (Figure 1A left) and individual cells (Figure 1B), in both monkeys (Figure 1C top) and mice (Figure 1C bottom, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Spike rate was correlated with gaze velocity during VOR cancellation in monkeys and mice.
source: Similarly, when monkeys or mice held their eyes roughly stationary relative to the head to track a visual stimulus that moved with the head, a behavior known as cancellation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, gaze velocity closely tracked head velocity, and spike rate was again correlated with gaze velocity (Figure 1A right, Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The same, roughly linear relationship between spike rate and gaze velocity was observed during eye movement responses to multiple combinations of visual and vestibular stimuli with different velocity profiles.
source: The same, roughly linear relationship between spike rate and gaze velocity was observed during eye movement responses to multiple combinations of visual and vestibular stimuli with different velocity profiles, and when the visual stimulus used to drive eye movements was a large-field visual stimulus (monkeys and mice) or a small visual target (monkeys only) (Figure 1C; mean correlation coefficient across conditions 0.81 ± 0.02, p=10−69, n = 120 cells, monkey; correlation coefficient 0.71 ± 0.04, p=10−19, n = 33 cells, mouse).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: Spike irregularity was correlated with gaze velocity across a range of visual and vestibular stimulus conditions in both monkeys and mice.
source: Like spike rate, spike irregularity was also correlated with gaze velocity across a range of visual and vestibular stimulus conditions in both monkeys and mice (Figure 1A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: During visual tracking and VOR cancellation, there was modulation of spike irregularity that mirrored the modulation of gaze velocity.
source: During visual tracking and VOR cancellation, there was modulation of spike irregularity that mirrored the modulation of gaze velocity, with CV2 increasing for gaze movements in one direction and decreasing for gaze movements in the other direction (Figure 1A, purple).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A roughly linear relationship between spike irregularity and gaze velocity was observed in individual Purkinje cells and in the population means recorded in monkeys and mice.
source: More generally, across the set of visual and vestibular stimulus conditions tested, a roughly linear relationship between spike irregularity and gaze velocity was observed in individual Purkinje cells (Figure 1B, bottom; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and in the population means (Figure 1D) recorded in monkeys and mice (mean correlation coefficient across conditions –0.53 ± 0.03, p = 10−38, n = 120 cells, monkey; –0.47 ± 0.05, p = 10−10, n = 33 cells, mouse).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and statistical analysis.

claim: Mean spike rate and mean irregularity covaried during oculomotor behavior.
source: However, the respective contributions of spike rate and irregularity could not be dissociated based on the responses quantified by averaging across trials, since mean spike rate and mean irregularity covaried.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Whenever mean spike rate was high, mean CV2 was lower (spike timing was more regular), and when mean spike rate was low, mean CV2 was high (spike timing was more irregular).
source: Whenever mean spike rate was high, mean CV2 was lower (spike timing was more regular), and when mean spike rate was low, mean CV2 was high (spike timing was more irregular) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The inverse relationship between spike rate and CV2 was observed in the Purkinje cells that encode ipsiversive gaze velocity and also in Purkinje cells with different responses to eye velocity or vestibular input.
source: The inverse relationship between spike rate and CV2 was observed in the Purkinje cells that encode ipsiversive gaze velocity, which make up the largest subset of Purkinje cells in the cerebellar flocculus (plotted in Figure 1), and also in Purkinje cells with different responses to eye velocity or vestibular input (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The covariation between spike rate and irregularity may reflect, in part, a tendency for the refractory period to cause spiking to be more regular at high rates.
source: This covariation between spike rate and irregularity may reflect, in part, a tendency for the refractory period to cause spiking to be more regular at high rates (Holt et al., 1996)
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Simulations of Poisson spiking with an imposed refractory period did not fully capture the correlation between spike rate and irregularity.
source: however, simulations of Poisson spiking with an imposed refractory period did not fully capture the correlation between spike rate and irregularity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; see Holt et al., 1996)
evidence: This is supported by simulations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several factors are thought to influence spike irregularity in Purkinje cells, including voltage-gated conductances and synaptic input.
source: and several additional factors are thought to influence spike irregularity in Purkinje cells, including voltage-gated conductances (Raman and Bean, 1997; Raman and Bean, 1999; Hoebeek et al., 2005; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Gao et al., 2012; Stahl and Thumser, 2014) and synaptic input (Häusser and Clark, 1997; Jaeger and Bower, 1999; Shin et al., 2007; Wulff et al., 2009; Jelitai et al., 2016; Peter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Over short timescales within individual trials, spike rate and CV2 did not covary strongly.
source: Indeed, over short timescales within individual trials, spike rate and CV2 did not covary strongly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residual spike rate, residual CV2, and residual eye velocity were calculated by subtracting the corresponding trial mean from the response on each individual trial, computed in 50 ms time bins.
source: For each Purkinje cell, residual spike rate, residual CV2, and residual eye velocity were calculated by subtracting the corresponding trial mean from the response on each individual trial, computed in 50 ms time bins (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method used.

claim: A linear mixed effects model found a significant contribution of residual spike rate, but not residual CV2, for predicting residual eye velocity in monkeys.
source: This analysis found a significant contribution of residual spike rate, but not residual CV2, for predicting residual eye velocity in monkeys (rate: p=0.006; CV2: p=0.56; interaction: p=0.17; likelihood ratio test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: A linear mixed effects model found a significant contribution of residual spike rate, but not residual CV2, for predicting residual eye velocity in mice.
source: This analysis found a significant contribution of residual spike rate, but not residual CV2, for predicting residual eye velocity in monkeys (rate: p=0.006; CV2: p=0.56; interaction: p=0.17; likelihood ratio test) and mice (rate: p=0.035; CV2: p=0.38; interaction: p=0.46)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Spike rate was a better predictor of moment-to-moment eye velocity than spike irregularity.
source: Spike rate was therefore a better predictor of moment-to-moment eye velocity than spike irregularity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the statistical analysis.

claim: There was a consistent correlation between residual spike rate and residual eye velocity.
source: There was a consistent correlation between residual spike rate and residual eye velocity (Figure 2C,D): on trials with higher than average spike rate at a particular time within the trial, eye velocity was also higher than average at that time within that trial.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: One extra spike in a 50 ms time bin, corresponding to a 20 sp/s fluctuation in spike rate, was associated with a roughly 0.1°/s change in eye velocity.
source: One extra spike in a 50 ms time bin, corresponding to a 20 sp/s fluctuation in spike rate, was associated with a roughly 0.1°/s change in eye velocity, consistent with the correlation between single spikes and visual tracking behavior reported by Chaisanguanthum et al. (2014).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, consistent with prior work.

claim: The same relationship between residual spike rate and eye velocity was observed for time bins with high or low CV2.
source: The same relationship between residual spike rate and eye velocity was observed for time bins with high or low CV2 (Figure 2C,D), consistent with the conclusion of the linear mixed effects model that spike irregularity did not substantially modulate the effects of spike rate on eye movements (no main effect of CV2 or interaction between spike rate and CV2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D and statistical analysis.

claim: When residual eye velocity was plotted against residual CV2, there was no correlation.
source: Moreover, when residual eye velocity was plotted against residual CV2, there was no correlation (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Moment-to-moment variations in eye velocity could be explained by moment-to-moment variations in spike rate, but not spike irregularity.
source: Therefore, although on average, both spike rate and irregularity were correlated with each other and with motor output during eye movement behaviors (Figure 1), moment-to-moment variations in eye velocity could be explained by moment-to-moment variations in spike rate, but not spike irregularity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: The recording results found no evidence that spike irregularity influenced motor output during oculomotor behavior.
source: Thus, the recording results found no evidence that spike irregularity influenced motor output during oculomotor behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the recording experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cells made it possible to independently manipulate spike rate and irregularity by delivering sequences of light pulses with different stimulus rates and irregularities.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cells made it possible to independently manipulate spike rate and irregularity by delivering sequences of light pulses with different stimulus rates and irregularities.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) was selectively expressed in Purkinje cells by crossing a conditional ChR2 mouse line with the L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line.
source: Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) was selectively expressed in Purkinje cells by crossing a conditional ChR2 mouse line (Madisen et al., 2012) with the L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line, which is highly selective for Purkinje cells (Zhang et al., 2004; Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the genetic approach used, supported by citations.

claim: The L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line is highly selective for Purkinje cells.
source: Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) was selectively expressed in Purkinje cells by crossing a conditional ChR2 mouse line (Madisen et al., 2012) with the L7/Pcp2-Cre Jdhu line, which is highly selective for Purkinje cells (Zhang et al., 2004; Witter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Purkinje cells expressing ChR2 were stimulated in vivo using 500 ms trains of 1 ms pulses of light delivered at mean rates from 20 Hz to 100 Hz.
source: Purkinje cells expressing ChR2 were stimulated in vivo using 500 ms trains of 1 ms pulses of light delivered at mean rates from 20 Hz to 100 Hz.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For a given mean rate, the exact same number of pulses were delivered during each train, with variations only in the irregularity of the stimulus pulse timing.
source: For a given mean rate, the exact same number of pulses were delivered during each train, with variations only in the irregularity of the stimulus pulse timing, so that the CV of each stimulus train was either 0 (perfectly regular), 0.5 (intermediate irregular), or 1 (approximately Poisson irregular) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Extracellular recordings confirmed that optogenetic stimulation effectively dissociated spike rate and irregularity in Purkinje cells in vivo.
source: Extracellular recordings confirmed that optogenetic stimulation effectively dissociated spike rate and irregularity in Purkinje cells in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the recording experiments during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Purkinje cells in the flocculus were identified based on their reliable, short-latency responses to 1 ms light pulses.
source: Purkinje cells in the flocculus were identified based on their reliable, short-latency responses to 1 ms light pulses (median first-spike latency 1.24 ± 0.07 ms, standard deviation 1.36 ± 0.17 ms, n = 13, 1 mW light intensity; Figure 3A–C)
evidence: This describes the identification criteria and is supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Purkinje cell identity was confirmed by their characteristic spike waveform, high-frequency spontaneous activity, and recording location within the layers of the cerebellar cortex.
source: and their identity was confirmed by their characteristic spike waveform (Figure 3A), high-frequency spontaneous activity (62.2 ± 6.9 sp/s, n = 13), and recording location within the layers of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This describes the confirmation criteria and is supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Purkinje cells responded to individual light pulses within each stimulus train.
source: Purkinje cells responded to individual light pulses within each stimulus train (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The increase in spike rate above baseline, averaged over the 500 ms stimulus period, followed the stimulus rate in a roughly 1:1 manner, even for stimulus rates as high as 100 Hz.
source: The increase in spike rate above baseline, averaged over the 500 ms stimulus period, followed the stimulus rate in a roughly 1:1 manner, even for stimulus rates as high as 100 Hz (Figure 3F,G, left).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Irregular stimulus trains drove slightly lower mean spike rates than regular trains.
source: Irregular stimulus trains drove slightly lower mean spike rates than regular trains (Figure 3G, left)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The overall irregularity of the combined spontaneous and optogenetically-driven Purkinje cell spikes consistently reflected the irregularity of the stimulus train.
source: Importantly, the overall irregularity of the combined spontaneous and optogenetically-driven Purkinje cell spikes consistently reflected the irregularity of the stimulus train (Figure 3F,G, right), with substantially more irregular spiking during the irregular stimulus trains compared to the regular stimulus trains.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation provided differential control of spike rate and spike irregularity in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: Thus, optogenetic stimulation provided differential control of spike rate and spike irregularity in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic recording experiments.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the Purkinje cells elicited robust eye movement responses.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of the Purkinje cells elicited robust eye movement responses.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Discrete eye movement responses could be observed in response to each light pulse, even at stimulus frequencies as high as 100 Hz.
source: Discrete eye movement responses could be observed in response to each light pulse, even at stimulus frequencies as high as 100 Hz (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Mean eye velocity increased with stimulus rate.
source: Like Purkinje cell spike rate, mean eye velocity increased with stimulus rate (Figure 4C,D), consistent with the Purkinje cells controlling eye velocity with a rate code.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: A similar correlation between stimulus rate and mean eye velocity was observed during both regular and irregular stimulus trains.
source: A similar correlation between stimulus rate and mean eye velocity was observed during both regular and irregular stimulus trains.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: The mean eye velocity evoked by irregular trains was slightly smaller than that evoked by regular trains.
source: The mean eye velocity evoked by irregular trains was slightly smaller than that evoked by regular trains; however, the mean Purkinje cell spike rate was also slightly smaller during irregular trains (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 4.

claim: When mean eye velocity was assessed as a function of the actual mean spike rate recorded in the Purkinje cells rather than the stimulation rate, there was no significant difference in the net efficacy of the regular and irregular spike trains to drive eye movements.
source: When mean eye velocity was assessed as a function of the actual mean spike rate recorded in the Purkinje cells rather than the stimulation rate, there was no significant difference in the net efficacy of the regular and irregular spike trains to drive eye movements (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis.

claim: The stimulation results do not support the prediction from previous studies that more irregular Purkinje cell spike trains should have less impact downstream than more regular spike trains.
source: Thus, our stimulation results do not support the prediction from previous studies that more irregular Purkinje cell spike trains should have less impact downstream than more regular spike trains (Luthman et al., 2011; Hoebeek et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic stimulation experiments, contrasting with prior predictions.

claim: The eye movement trajectories clearly depended on the exact temporal pattern of stimulation, with eye movements tracking the occurrence of individual stimuli within the train.
source: On a finer timescale, the eye movement trajectories clearly depended on the exact temporal pattern of stimulation, with eye movements tracking the occurrence of individual stimuli within the train (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The moment-to-moment eye movement trajectories could be well accounted for as a rapid, linear response of the eye to changes in the Purkinje cell population spike rate.
source: However, additional analysis demonstrated that these moment-to-moment eye movement trajectories could be well accounted for as a rapid, linear response of the eye to changes in the Purkinje cell population spike rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the linear filter modeling analysis.

claim: Mutual information was maximal when spike rate and eye velocity were smoothed over a temporal window of 3–5 ms.
source: For both regular and irregular stimulus trains, mutual information was maximal when spike rate and eye velocity were smoothed over a temporal window of 3–5 ms (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Purkinje cell population transmits a rate code that is decoded by the oculomotor circuitry on a timescale of 3–5 ms.
source: Thus, the Purkinje cell population transmits a rate code that is decoded by the oculomotor circuitry on a timescale of 3–5 ms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutual information analysis.

claim: For rapid timescales encompassing the optimal decoding window of 3–5 ms, the same amount of information about eye movements was transmitted by the Purkinje cell rate code during regular and irregular stimulation.
source: Importantly, for rapid timescales encompassing this optimal decoding window of 3–5 ms, the same amount of information about eye movements was transmitted by the Purkinje cell rate code during regular and irregular stimulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Spike irregularity did not alter the magnitude of the influence of spike rate on eye movements.
source: Spike irregularity therefore did not alter the magnitude of the influence of spike rate on eye movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutual information analysis.

claim: The transformation between population spike rate and eye velocity could be described by the same linear temporal filter.
source: Not only did the instantaneous spike rate carry the same amount of information about eye velocity irrespective of spike irregularity, but the transformation between population spike rate and eye velocity could be described by the same linear temporal filter.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the linear filter modeling.

claim: The linear filter model closely predicted eye velocity with root mean squared error (RMSE) that did not differ significantly between the regular and irregular test stimulus trains.
source: The linear filter model closely predicted eye velocity (Figure 5C,D) with root mean squared error (RMSE) that did not differ significantly between the regular and irregular test stimulus trains (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-E and statistical analysis.

claim: When the model was fit to data from the regular stimulation at all frequencies, the resulting linear filter was nearly identical to the filter fit to the irregular data only.
source: Further, when the model was fit to data from the regular stimulation at all frequencies (20, 40, 60, 80, 100 Hz), the resulting linear filter was nearly identical to the filter fit to the irregular data only (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The same linear filter model described the relationship between spike rate and motor output equally well, regardless of the underlying spike pattern.
source: Thus, the same linear filter model described the relationship between spike rate and motor output equally well, regardless of the underlying spike pattern.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the linear filter modeling.

claim: Highly irregular spiking in individual Purkinje cells may degrade the precision of the motor commands carried by the population rate, by increasing its moment-to-moment and trial-to-trial variability.
source: In particular, highly irregular spiking in individual Purkinje cells may degrade the precision of the motor commands carried by the population rate, by increasing its moment-to-moment and trial-to-trial variability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by simulation.

claim: Higher spike irregularity increased the moment-to-moment variation in the population rate from the specified rate, as demonstrated by a broadening of the distribution of instantaneous population rates.
source: Higher spike irregularity increased the moment-to-moment variation in the population rate from the specified rate, as demonstrated by a broadening of the distribution of instantaneous population rates (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The broadening of the population rate distribution was subtle for variations in spike irregularity in the normal range observed in the recording and stimulation experiments and in previous studies of Purkinje cells in wild type mice.
source: This broadening was subtle for variations in spike irregularity in the normal range observed in our recording and stimulation experiments and in previous studies of Purkinje cells in wild type mice (Figure 6A, blue and red; Gao et al., 2012; Stahl and Thumser, 2014; Mark et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and citations to prior work.

claim: The broadening of the population rate distribution was more pronounced for the higher levels of irregularity that have been reported in mouse models of ataxia.
source: but was more pronounced for the higher levels of irregularity that have been reported in mouse models of ataxia (Figure 6A, purple; Hoebeek et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2006; Luthman et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2012; Stahl and Thumser, 2014; Mark et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6A and citations to prior work.

claim: The area under the ROC curve decreased with higher spike irregularity in the individual Purkinje cells, indicating decreased ability to discriminate distinct motor commands conveyed by the population spike rate.
source: The area under the ROC curve decreased with higher spike irregularity in the individual Purkinje cells, indicating decreased ability to discriminate distinct motor commands conveyed by the population spike rate (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Pathological levels of spike irregularity may cause ataxia, not through a direct effect of the irregularity itself, but by degrading the accuracy of the rapid rate code carried by Purkinje cells.
source: This provides a potential reconciliation of our current finding of a rapid rate code for motor control with previous reports in ataxic mice suggesting that abnormally high irregularity of Purkinje cell spike trains disrupts normal downstream signaling and motor output (Hoebeek et al., 2005; Walter et al., 2006; Wulff et al., 2009; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010b; Alviña and Khodakhah, 2010a; Luthman et al., 2011). Pathological levels of spike irregularity may cause ataxia, not through a direct effect of the irregularity itself, but by degrading the accuracy of the rapid rate code carried by Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to reconcile current findings with prior work.

claim: A previous study using a conductance-based model indicated that more irregular Purkinje cell spike trains should be less effective, on average, than regular spike trains at inhibiting postsynaptic targets.
source: A previous study using this model indicated that more irregular Purkinje cell spike trains should be less effective, on average, than regular spike trains at inhibiting postsynaptic targets (Luthman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior modeling work.

claim: When model parameters were identical to those previously published, the model predicted that irregular stimulus trains would have substantially smaller net impact on mean target neuron output than regular stimulus trains.
source: When model parameters were identical to those previously published (Luthman et al., 2011), the model predicted that irregular stimulus trains (CV = 1) would have substantially smaller net impact on mean target neuron output than regular stimulus trains (CV = 0) (Figure 7C1), as previously reported for simulations of spontaneous Purkinje cell spiking with different levels of irregularity.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7C1 and citation to prior work.

claim: The in vivo observations could not be explained by the previously chosen model parameters.
source: This prediction was inconsistent with our experimental observation of similar net impact of regular and irregular spike trains on eye movements (Figure 4); thus the in vivo observations could not be explained by the previously chosen model parameters.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing model predictions with experimental data.

claim: Changes to specific model parameters within a biologically realistic range allowed the model to reproduce the experimental results.
source: We found that changes to specific model parameters within a biologically realistic range allowed the model to reproduce the experimental results.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: Short-term plasticity at synapses from Purkinje cells to their target neurons is developmentally regulated, such that synaptic transmission in adult mice is remarkably independent of spike rate.
source: However, it was recently discovered that short-term plasticity at these synapses is developmentally regulated, such that synaptic transmission in adult mice is remarkably independent of spike rate (Turecek et al., 2016; Turecek et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Elimination of short-term depression was not sufficient to allow the model to reproduce the experimentally observed responses to optogenetic stimulus trains.
source: However, elimination of short-term depression was not sufficient to allow the model to reproduce the experimentally observed responses to optogenetic stimulus trains (Figure 7C2).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 7C2.

claim: Even without short-term depression, the model predicted smaller net impact of irregular than regular stimulus trains, contrary to the experimental observations.
source: Even without short-term depression, the model predicted smaller net impact of irregular than regular stimulus trains, contrary to the experimental observations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The biophysics of the Purkinje cell-target neuron synapses are consistent with a negligible effect of Purkinje cell spike irregularity.
source: Thus, although previous work with the same biophysical model contended that spike irregularity should affect downstream processing of the Purkinje cells' output (Luthman et al., 2011), the biophysics of the Purkinje cell-target neuron synapses are also consistent with a negligible effect of Purkinje cell spike irregularity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The recording, stimulation, and modeling results make a strong case that floccular Purkinje cells control eye movements with a rapid population rate code, with no evidence for an additional effect of spike irregularity.
source: Taken together, the recording, stimulation, and modeling results make a strong case that floccular Purkinje cells control eye movements with a rapid population rate code, with no evidence for an additional effect of spike irregularity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A range of relationships between spike irregularity and mean target neuron output can arise from even the most basic features of a neuron: a spike threshold, a post-spike reset membrane potential, and a minimum membrane potential, combined with stochastic inputs.
source: A much simpler, random walk model (Gerstein and Mandelbrot, 1964; Shadlen and Newsome, 1998; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000) reveals that a range of relationships between spike irregularity and mean target neuron output can arise from even the most basic features of a neuron: a spike threshold, a post-spike reset membrane potential, and a minimum membrane potential, combined with stochastic inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the random walk modeling.

claim: In the random walk model, the effect of increased input variance on the target neuron spike rate depended on the location in parameter space.
source: Even in the extremely simple random walk model, the effect of increased input variance on the target neuron spike rate depended on the location in parameter space (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 9.

claim: An increase in input variance can drive a higher spike rate in the target neuron.
source: A well-known prior result (Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000) is that an increase in input variance can drive a higher spike rate in the target neuron (Figure 9B, positive slopes).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 9B and a citation to prior work.

claim: An increase in input variance can decrease spike rate in the target neuron.
source: A less recognized finding from the random walk model is that it can also exhibit the opposite behavior, whereby an increase in input variance can decrease spike rate in the target neuron (Figure 9B, negative slopes; see also Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 9B and a citation to prior work.

claim: With other model parameters held constant, as input variance increases from zero, the spike rate can first decrease and then increase.
source: Indeed, with other model parameters held constant, as input variance increases from zero, the spike rate can first decrease and then increase (Figure 9B, black and red).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: In the transition between regimes where variance increases or decreases spike rate, changes in input variance within a certain, intermediate range have minimal effect on spike rate in the target neuron.
source: In the transition between these two regimes, changes in input variance within a certain, intermediate range have minimal effect on spike rate in the target neuron (Figure 9B, flat portion of the curves).
evidence: This is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The experiments appear to have uncovered a biological example of an overlooked region of parameter space, where changes in synaptic input variability within the range experienced during normal behavior have little impact and hence do not interfere with the rate code for motor output.
source: Our experiments appear to have uncovered a biological example of an overlooked region of parameter space, where changes in synaptic input variability within the range experienced during normal behavior have little impact and hence do not interfere with the rate code for motor output.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating experimental and modeling results.

claim: The results suggest that the transformation of Purkinje cell activity into motor output is closely approximated by a rapid population rate code.
source: The results suggest that the transformation of Purkinje cell activity into motor output is closely approximated by a rapid population rate code (Figure 10).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Natural, trial-to-trial variations in the eye movement responses to repetitions of the same stimuli could be predicted from fluctuations in spike rate, but not from fluctuations in spike irregularity.
source: However, natural, trial-to-trial variations in the eye movement responses to repetitions of the same stimuli could be predicted from fluctuations in spike rate, but not from fluctuations in spike irregularity (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The ability to predict fluctuations in behavior from the spike rate recorded in a single Purkinje cell suggests that the fluctuations in spike rate are shared across a large fraction of the population of Purkinje cells that control eye movements.
source: The ability to predict fluctuations in behavior from the spike rate recorded in a single Purkinje cell suggests that the fluctuations in spike rate are shared across a large fraction of the population of Purkinje cells that control eye movements (see also Chaisanguanthum et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The lack of correlation between fluctuations in CV2 and eye velocity could indicate that the effect of spike irregularity in a single neuron is too small to detect, and fluctuations in spike irregularity are not shared across the population of Purkinje cells.
source: In contrast, the lack of correlation between fluctuations in CV2 and eye velocity could indicate that 1) the effect of spike irregularity in a single neuron is too small to detect, and fluctuations in spike irregularity are not shared across the population of Purkinje cells, or 2) spike irregularity does not influence eye velocity.
evidence: This is a possible interpretation of the data.

claim: The lack of correlation between fluctuations in CV2 and eye velocity could indicate that spike irregularity does not influence eye velocity.
source: In contrast, the lack of correlation between fluctuations in CV2 and eye velocity could indicate that 1) the effect of spike irregularity in a single neuron is too small to detect, and fluctuations in spike irregularity are not shared across the population of Purkinje cells, or 2) spike irregularity does not influence eye velocity.
evidence: This is a possible interpretation of the data.

claim: The results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments favor the interpretation that spike irregularity does not influence eye velocity.
source: The results from the optogenetic stimulation experiments favor the latter interpretation, since the optogenetic stimulus trains drove robust changes in spike irregularity across a large population of stimulated Purkinje cells, yet there was no difference in the mean eye velocity during regular and irregular spike trains after controlling for spike rate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: The levels of synchrony across the Purkinje cell population during optogenetic stimulation were almost certainly higher than during natural behavior.
source: The levels of synchrony across the Purkinje cell population during optogenetic stimulation were almost certainly higher than during natural behavior
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental conditions.

claim: The biophysical model predicts even smaller effects of spike irregularity under conditions of lower synchrony.
source: however, the biophysical model predicts even smaller effects of spike irregularity under conditions of lower synchrony, consistent with the recordings made under conditions of natural levels of synchrony (Figure 2), which also yielded no evidence for an impact of spike irregularity.
evidence: This is supported by modeling results and consistency with recording data.

claim: The convergent evidence from the complementary recording, stimulation, and modeling approaches indicates that the irregularity of spiking in Purkinje cells is not a significant component of the code used by the cerebellar flocculus to control normal eye movements.
source: Taken together, the convergent evidence from the complementary recording, stimulation, and modeling approaches indicates that the irregularity of spiking in Purkinje cells is not a significant component of the code used by the cerebellar flocculus to control normal eye movements.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The recording and stimulation results can be fully accounted for by the Purkinje cells controlling eye movements primarily or exclusively via a rate code.
source: The recording and stimulation results can be fully accounted for by the Purkinje cells controlling eye movements primarily or exclusively via a rate code.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that electrical or optogenetic manipulation of Purkinje cell activity can drive motor responses, with bigger behavioral responses for higher intensity stimulation.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that electrical or optogenetic manipulation of Purkinje cell activity can drive motor responses, with bigger behavioral responses for higher intensity stimulation (Ron and Robinson, 1973; Belknap and Noda, 1987; Lisberger, 1994; Wada et al., 2014; Nguyen-Vu et al., 2013; Heiney et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2015; Stahl et al., 2015; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The current study extended prior work by showing a roughly linear relationship between Purkinje cell spike rate and behavior for optogenetic stimulation-driven spike rates from 0 to 100 sp/s above the spontaneous rate.
source: We extended this work by showing a roughly linear relationship between Purkinje cell spike rate and behavior for optogenetic stimulation-driven spike rates from 0 to 100 sp/s above the spontaneous rate (Figure 4E), consistent with the linear coding described in recordings of neural activity during oculomotor behavior (Figure 1C; Shidara and Kawano, 1993; Lisberger, 1994; Kahlon and Lisberger, 1999; Medina and Lisberger, 2007; Medina and Lisberger, 2009; Katoh et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2016; Herzfeld et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2017; reviewed in Raymond and Medina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and citations to prior work.

claim: Previous work has shown that inhibitory synaptic transmission between Purkinje cells and their postsynaptic targets is fast, with a synaptic time constant of 2 ms.
source: Previous work has shown that inhibitory synaptic transmission between Purkinje cells and their postsynaptic targets is fast, with a synaptic time constant of 2 ms (Najac and Raman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The speed of synaptic transmission is largely maintained in the downstream oculomotor circuitry.
source: We found that this speed is largely maintained in the downstream oculomotor circuitry, which includes signaling from the flocculus target neurons in the vestibular nuclei to their interneuron and motor neuron targets in the abducens nucleus, and the effects of the latter on the oculomotor plant (reviewed in Highstein et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the current study, with a citation to a review.

claim: The population spike rate in the floccular Purkinje cells appears to be read out by the downstream oculomotor circuitry on a timescale of 3–5 ms.
source: Thus, the population spike rate in the floccular Purkinje cells appears to be read out by the downstream oculomotor circuitry on a timescale of 3–5 ms.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the mutual information and linear filter analyses.

claim: 3–5 ms is less than the typical ISI in an individual Purkinje cell, but is a reasonable timescale for considering the population spike rate in the ~50 Purkinje cells converging on a given target.
source: This is less than the typical ISI in an individual Purkinje cell, but is a reasonable timescale for considering the population spike rate in the ~50 Purkinje cells converging on a given target, which will collectively emit 10 or more spikes, on average, per 5 ms interval
evidence: This is an inference about the biological relevance of the timescale.

claim: Rapid rate coding is likely not unique to the oculomotor system; there is evidence that other motor circuits can transmit information on a similar timescale.
source: Such rapid rate coding is likely not unique to the oculomotor system; there is evidence that other motor circuits can transmit information on a similar timescale (Tang et al., 2014; Srivastava et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The rapid speed at which the population spike rate is read out could endow the circuit with sensitivity to any spiking statistics that alter the population rate over short timescales, including spike irregularity and synchrony.
source: The rapid speed at which the population spike rate is read out could endow the circuit with sensitivity to any spiking statistics that alter the population rate over short timescales, including spiking statistics that are typically associated with temporal coding, such as spike irregularity and synchrony (Figure 10).
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of rapid rate coding.

claim: The convergence of ~50 Purkinje cells onto each target neuron can average out the 'noisiness' of signals carried by the spike trains of individual neurons.
source: The convergence of ~50 Purkinje cells onto each target neuron can average out the 'noisiness' of signals carried by the spike trains of individual neurons.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional consequence of convergence.

claim: This averaging out needs to occur on a timescale of 3–5 ms, because variations in the population rate get faithfully transmitted all the way to the behavior with this temporal resolution.
source: Our results indicate that this averaging out needs to occur on a timescale of 3–5 ms, because variations in the population rate get faithfully transmitted all the way to the behavior with this temporal resolution (Figure 5, Figure 10C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: The high level of Purkinje cell spike irregularity in ataxia could degrade the accuracy of movements by degrading the accuracy and precision of the motor commands carried by the population spike rate.
source: This provides a mechanism by which the high level of Purkinje cell spike irregularity in ataxia (CV of 0.7–2.3 in ataxic mice compared to 0.4–0.6 in control mice; Hoebeek et al., 2005; Gao et al., 2012; Stahl and Thumser, 2014; Mark et al., 2015) could degrade the accuracy of movements: by degrading the accuracy and precision of the motor commands carried by the population spike rate (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by simulations and citations to prior work.

claim: Smaller variations in spike irregularity within the normal physiological range may be well tolerated because they have minimal impact on the population spike rate.
source: In contrast, smaller variations in spike irregularity within the normal physiological range may be well tolerated because they have minimal impact on the population spike rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: Purkinje cell synchrony can be reframed as rapid changes in the Purkinje cell population firing rate on a timescale of a few milliseconds, which could be transmitted downstream via the rapid population rate code for eye velocity.
source: Similarly, Purkinje cell synchrony (Bell and Grimm, 1969; Bell and Kawasaki, 1972; Ebner and Bloedel, 1981; Shin and De Schutter, 2006; Heck et al., 2007; de Solages et al., 2008; Wise et al., 2010; Person and Raman, 2012a; Sarnaik and Raman, 2018; Brown and Raman, 2018; Tang et al., 2019) can be reframed as rapid changes in the Purkinje cell population firing rate on a timescale of a few milliseconds, which could be transmitted downstream via the rapid population rate code for eye velocity.
evidence: This is an inference about how synchrony relates to the rate code, supported by citations.

claim: Rapid fluctuations in the population rate, which can be generated by spike irregularity or synchrony, can be read out as rapid fluctuations in the intended motor command.
source: Thus, rapid fluctuations in the population rate, which can be generated by spike irregularity or synchrony, can be read out as rapid fluctuations in the intended motor command (Figure 10), allowing spike irregularity and synchrony to influence behavior via the rate code.
evidence: This is a conclusion about how irregularity and synchrony can influence behavior through the rate code.

claim: It is important to distinguish rapid rate coding from true temporal coding.
source: Extremely rapid rate coding might seem to blur the line between rate coding and temporal coding, but it is important to distinguish rapid rate coding from true temporal coding.
evidence: This is a conceptual clarification.

claim: The term 'temporal coding' should be reserved to refer to an influence of the temporal statistics of spiking that cannot be accounted for by the population spike rate computed over a biologically relevant timescale.
source: Although the term 'temporal code' is sometimes used to describe changes in spike rate co-occurring with changes in a dynamic stimulus or behavior (e.g. Gooler and Feng, 1992), we would reserve the term 'temporal coding' to refer to an influence of the temporal statistics of spiking that cannot be accounted for by the population spike rate computed over a biologically relevant timescale (Theunissen and Miller, 1995).
evidence: This is a conceptual definition supported by citations.

claim: The current study found no evidence for temporal coding in the rigorous sense of the term.
source: We found no evidence for temporal coding in the latter, more rigorous sense of the term.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: The current study does not rule out other forms of temporal coding in the cerebellar circuit.
source: Temporal coding could potentially take many forms, and we evaluated just one form based on spike irregularity, hence our results do not rule out other forms of temporal coding in the cerebellar circuit.
evidence: This acknowledges the limitations of the study.

claim: The experiments were designed specifically to detect effects of spike irregularity above and beyond what could be accounted for by a population rate code for eye velocity, and no evidence for such effects was found.
source: Our experiments were designed specifically to detect effects of spike irregularity above and beyond what could be accounted for by a population rate code for eye velocity, and we found no evidence for such effects.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental design and findings.

claim: The irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking in the flocculus can affect the fine temporal structure of movement through a rapid rate code, without the need to invoke a separate temporal code.
source: Thus the irregularity of Purkinje cell spiking in the flocculus can affect the fine temporal structure of movement through a rapid rate code, without the need to invoke a separate temporal code.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: It is possible that the impact of spike irregularity in Purkinje cells could vary across different zones or microzones of the cerebellum.
source: It is possible that the impact of spike irregularity in Purkinje cells could vary across different zones or microzones of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential differences across cerebellar regions.

claim: There is substantial variation in the gene expression, firing rates, and properties of synaptic plasticity in the Purkinje cells in different areas of the cerebellar cortex.
source: There is substantial variation in the gene expression, firing rates, and properties of synaptic plasticity in the Purkinje cells in different areas of the cerebellar cortex (Suvrathan et al., 2016; Cerminara et al., 2015; Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Kim et al., 2012; Witter and De Zeeuw, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is substantial variation in the properties of Purkinje cells' target neurons in different deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei.
source: and in the Purkinje cells' target neurons in different deep cerebellar and vestibular nuclei (Chan-Palay, 1977; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Sugihara, 2011; Sekirnjak and du Lac, 2006; Pugh and Raman, 2006; Bagnall et al., 2007; McElvain et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2011; Low et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The biophysical modeling indicates that variations in model parameters within a biologically plausible range could determine whether spike irregularity either does or does not influence the transmission of information by the Purkinje cells.
source: Our biophysical modeling indicates that variations in model parameters within a biologically plausible range could determine whether spike irregularity either does or does not influence the transmission of information by the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: The cerebellar flocculus operates in a region of parameter space where the impact of spike irregularity is negligible, even during highly synchronous population activity.
source: Although recording and stimulation results indicate that the cerebellar flocculus operates in a region of parameter space where the impact of spike irregularity is negligible, even during highly synchronous population activity
evidence: This is a conclusion from the recording and stimulation experiments.

claim: Changing a single parameter, such as the ratio of excitation to inhibition, could create sensitivity to spike irregularity.
source: the model demonstrates that changing a single parameter, such as the ratio of excitation to inhibition, could create sensitivity to spike irregularity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: Other parts of the cerebellum may operate in regions of parameter space where spike irregularity has an impact beyond what can be accounted for by the rapid rate code.
source: Thus, other parts of the cerebellum may operate in regions of parameter space where spike irregularity has an impact beyond what can be accounted for by the rapid rate code.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Regular, synchronous optogenetic stimulus trains delivered to Purkinje cells of the cerebellar lobulus simplex were less likely to perturb ongoing locomotion than continuous optogenetic stimulation.
source: Some support for this possibility is provided by a recent report that regular, synchronous optogenetic stimulus trains delivered to Purkinje cells of the cerebellar lobulus simplex were less likely to perturb ongoing locomotion than continuous optogenetic stimulation, which elicits less regular, less synchronous spiking (Sarnaik and Raman, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A clear understanding of how the rate code influences behavior on a moment-to-moment basis is critical for evaluating the possibility that additional, temporal coding might also influence behavior.
source: Our finding that the population spike rate can influence behavior with high temporal precision demonstrates that a clear understanding of how the rate code influences behavior on a moment-to-moment basis is critical for evaluating the possibility that additional, temporal coding might also influence behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the importance of understanding rate coding.

claim: Additional research is required to determine what, if any, role spike irregularity or other forms of temporal coding play in the cerebellar control of complex behaviors such as locomotion.
source: Such analyses are more challenging for complex behaviors such as locomotion, hence additional research is required to determine what, if any, role spike irregularity or other forms of temporal coding play in the cerebellar control of such behaviors.
evidence: This acknowledges the need for future research.

claim: Understanding how information is transmitted through the rate and timing of spikes is central to understanding neural computation.
